metadata.title: A progenitor binary and an ejected mass donor remnant of faint type Ia supernovae

evidence.quote: This enigmatic star (US 708) has been classified as helium-rich hot subdwarf travelling at a Galactic rest frame velocity of at least 750 km s−1 (Hirsch et al. 2005), which matches the predicted ejection velocity of CD−30◦11223 very well.
The predicted properties of this remnant are an excellent match to the so-called hypervelocity star US 708, a hot, helium-rich star moving at more than 750 km s−1, suficient to leave the Galaxy.

Such so-called hypervelocity stars have indeed been discovered (Brown et al. 2005; Hirsch et al. 2005; Edelmann et al. 2005). However, all but one of the known 22 objects are intermediate-mass main-sequence star. This enigmatic star (US 708) has been classified as helium-rich hot subdwarf travelling at a Galactic rest frame velocity of at least 750 km s−1 (Hirsch et al. 2005), which matches the predicted ejection velocity of CD−30◦11223 very well.
In this scenario, the compact binary CD−30◦11223 and the hypervelocity star US 708 represent two diferent stages of an evolutionary sequence linked by a SN Ia explosion.

notes: US 708 is the only individually identified star that the paper treats as a Galactic unbound/hypervelocity object and studies as the likely ejected donor remnant; its unbound status is supported by the stated Galactic rest-frame velocity of at least 750 km s−1 being sufficient to leave the Galaxy. CD−30°11223 and its sdB/white-dwarf components are present-day bound binary members and are discussed as future SN Ia progenitors; their predicted future ejection does not make them present-day Galactic unbound candidates. KPD 1930+2752 is mentioned only as an SN Ia progenitor candidate, not as a Galactic unbound candidate.

US 708: US 708 is discussed as the proposed ejected donor remnant and comparison object, not as a system whose position, parallax, distance, or proper motion is measured in this paper. The only retained quantity is its reported Galactic rest-frame velocity lower limit. The abstract states “more than 750 km s−1,” while the discussion cites “at least 750 km s−1” from Hirsch et al. (2005); these are consistent as a lower limit (T:p1-b5, T:p6-b2).
